name: Upside-down hair washing

lead:
Upside-down hair washing means bending forward under the shower so hair falls toward the floor while shampooing and rinsing. It spread on TikTok as a way to get a deeper clean and more volume.
The appearance goal is fuller, cleaner-looking hair, especially for fine hair. Stylists quoted in lifestyle coverage say it may help volume and reach neglected areas at the back of the head; no source reviewed supports a hair-growth effect.

paras: People tip the head forward while washing and rinsing, then sometimes towel-dry upside down. It is often confused with "reverse hair washing", which means conditioning before shampooing.
Coverage describes few risks: water running into the face or nose, extra effort, and possible strain from bending for long. Vigorous rubbing of strands can cause damage.

web.title: Is Washing Your Hair Upside Down Really Beneficial?

chain: Hair lifts at the roots and the back of the head is reached
angle.text: People use it for volume and cleaner roots. Stylists quoted in coverage say it may suit fine hair.

lead: Upside-down hair washing is a TikTok-era technique in which the head is bent forward under the shower while shampooing and rinsing.[1] It is often discussed alongside reverse hair washing, a different method of conditioning first and shampooing mainly the roots.[2]

Claimed benefits in coverage include thorough cleansing, more volume for finer hair, less friction between strands and fewer products running over the back and neck skin.[1] Hair and makeup expert Aaron Barry notes people often rush the back of the head.[1]
Coverage relies on stylist and editor opinion rather than clinical studies.[1][2]

paras: The head is bent forward under running water to shampoo and rinse; Zoe Weiner suggests wetting hair normally first to reduce water in the nose, and Christophe Robin recommends detangling and towel-drying upside down.[1]
The article names thorough cleansing, volume for fine hair, a clearer back and neck, and less friction as claimed benefits; Pureology's Jamie Wiley says it may be beneficial.[1]

Reverse washing, popularised on TikTok by Tessa Peay, uses conditioner first. Stylist Cody Renegar and Melanin Haircare's Whitney White say conditioner can benefit the ends; some commenters say it wastes product. Over-washing can strip scalp oils.[2]
